description: Congee with Century Egg is a quintessential Chinese comfort food, a savory rice porridge often enjoyed for breakfast or as a light meal. Its creamy texture combined with the unique, umami flavor of century eggs and often tender pork creates a truly satisfying experience. This traditional dish is known for its heartwarming qualities and distinct taste that transports you straight to a bustling Chinese kitchen.

instructions.title: Prepare the Rice
instructions.text: Wash the white rice thoroughly under cold running water until the water runs clear. For an extra creamy congee, you can soak the rice for 30 minutes prior to cooking, or even freeze it overnight.

instructions.title: Prepare Pork (Optional)
instructions.text: If using pork, slice the lean pork into very thin strips or small cubes. Marinate it in a small bowl with a pinch of salt, white pepper, and a dash of sesame oil for about 10 minutes to enhance its flavor and tenderness.

instructions.title: Cook the Congee Base
instructions.text: In a large heavy-bottomed pot, combine the washed rice with 8-10 cups of water or chicken broth. Bring the mixture to a rolling boil over high heat, then immediately reduce the heat to very low. Cover the pot and simmer gently for at least 35 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom.

instructions.title: Prepare Century Eggs
instructions.text: While the congee simmers, carefully peel the century eggs. Rinse them briefly under cold water to remove any residue. Cut each century egg into small wedges or dice them into roughly 1/2-inch pieces.

instructions.title: Combine Ingredients
instructions.text: Once the congee has reached your desired creamy consistency, add the prepared century egg pieces and the marinated pork (if using) to the pot. Stir everything well to combine. Continue to cook for another 5-7 minutes, or until the pork is fully cooked through and the eggs are heated.

instructions.title: Season and Serve
instructions.text: Taste the congee and season generously with salt and white pepper to your preference. Ladle the hot congee into individual serving bowls. Garnish each bowl with plenty of finely julienned fresh ginger and chopped green onions. Drizzle a few drops of sesame oil over the top just before serving for an authentic touch.

tips: For an extra creamy congee, freeze the washed rice overnight before cooking. The freezing and thawing process breaks down the rice grains, allowing them to cook into a smoother porridge faster.
Adding a small piece of pork rind or a tablespoon of peanut oil to the congee base while simmering can add a subtle richness and glossiness to the porridge.

Congee is best served immediately. If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop, adding a splash of water or broth if it has thickened too much.
article:
The gentle aroma of simmering rice, the promise of a warm, comforting bowl – few dishes evoke the feeling of home and nourishment quite like congee. A staple in Chinese cuisine, this savory rice porridge is a versatile canvas for countless flavors and ingredients. Among its most iconic and beloved iterations is Congee with Century Egg, a dish that masterfully balances unique textures and deep, umami-rich flavors, making it a quintessential Chinese breakfast experience. If you've ever dreamt of recreating this classic comfort food in your own kitchen, you're in the right place. This article will guide you through everything you need to know to prepare a delicious and authentic bowl of Congee with Century Egg, transforming your mornings into a culinary journey.

## What is Congee with Century Egg?
At its heart, congee is a simple rice porridge, often cooked until the grains break down into a creamy, almost soupy consistency. It’s revered across Asia as a breakfast food, a light meal, and even a soothing remedy for an upset stomach. Congee with Century Egg, known in Mandarin as "Pidan Shou Rou Zhou" (century egg and shredded pork congee), elevates this basic foundation with the addition of two distinct and flavorful ingredients: century eggs and shredded pork.

Century eggs, or "pidan," are a Chinese delicacy made by preserving duck, chicken, or quail eggs in a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime, and rice hulls for several weeks or months. This preservation process transforms the egg, giving the albumen a translucent, jelly-like texture and a dark, often marbled appearance, while the yolk turns a creamy, dark green or gray with a pungent, ammoniacal, and intensely savory flavor. When combined with tender shredded pork and a velvety smooth congee base, the century egg contributes a complex umami depth and a surprising creaminess that is both intriguing and incredibly satisfying. The dish is a symphony of textures and tastes, celebrated for its unique character and comforting warmth.

## Ingredients You Need
Creating an authentic Congee with Century Egg starts with selecting the right ingredients. Don't be intimidated by the century egg; it's readily available in most Asian supermarkets.

For a batch serving 4-6 people, you will need:
*   **1 cup Jasmine Rice or short-grain white rice:** Washed thoroughly.
*   **8-10 cups Water or Chicken Broth:** Broth adds a richer flavor.
*   **3-4 Century Eggs:** Peeled and diced into small pieces.
*   **8 oz Lean Pork Loin or Shoulder:** Shredded thinly.
*   **1 inch Fresh Ginger:** Peeled and julienned (shredded into thin strips).
*   **2-3 Green Onions (Scallions):** Chopped, for garnish.
*   **1 teaspoon Salt:** Or to taste.
*   **1/2 teaspoon White Pepper:** Or to taste.
*   **1 tablespoon Sesame Oil:** For drizzling.
*   **For Pork Marinade (optional but recommended):** 1 tsp cornstarch, 1 tsp light soy sauce, pinch of white pepper.

**Optional Garnishes:**
*   A dash of light soy sauce
*   Chili oil for a spicy kick
*   Crispy fried shallots or garlic
*   Fresh cilantro

## Step-by-Step Instructions
Making creamy, flavorful Congee with Century Egg is a straightforward process, though it requires a bit of patience for the rice to break down.

1.  **Prepare the Rice:** Rinse the rice under cold water several times until the water runs clear. For an even creamier congee and faster cooking time, you can soak the rice in water for at least 30 minutes, or even overnight.
2.  **Cook the Congee Base:** In a large, heavy-bottomed pot, combine the washed rice and 8 cups of water or chicken broth. Bring the mixture to a rolling boil over high heat. Once boiling, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, cover the pot partially (leaving a small gap for steam to escape), and simmer for 1 to 1.5 hours. Stir occasionally, especially towards the bottom, to prevent the rice from sticking and burning. The goal is for the rice grains to completely break down and create a thick, creamy porridge. If the congee becomes too thick, add more hot water or broth, a little at a time, until you reach your desired consistency.
3.  **Prepare the Pork:** While the congee simmers, prepare the pork. If using, marinate the shredded pork with cornstarch, light soy sauce, and white pepper for 10-15 minutes. This helps tenderize the meat. You can either blanch the pork quickly in boiling water until just cooked through, or add it directly to the congee in the final stage of cooking.
4.  **Prepare Century Eggs and Ginger:** Carefully peel the century eggs. The easiest way is to crack them gently all around, then peel under running water to remove any stubborn bits. Dice the peeled century eggs into small, bite-sized pieces. Prepare your julienned ginger and chopped green onions.
5.  **Combine and Season:** During the last 15-20 minutes of the congee’s cooking time, add the diced century eggs and the cooked (or blanched) shredded pork to the pot. Stir them gently into the congee, allowing their flavors to meld. Season generously with salt and white pepper to taste. The century eggs contribute a natural saltiness, so taste before adding too much.
6.  **Serve:** Ladle the hot Congee with Century Egg into individual bowls. Garnish each serving with fresh julienned ginger, chopped green onions, and a drizzle of sesame oil. Serve immediately.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results
Achieving that perfect bowl of Congee with Century Egg involves a few tricks of the trade:

*   **Rice Selection:** While Jasmine rice works well, some chefs prefer short-grain or even "old" rice (rice that has been stored for a while) for its ability to break down more easily and create a creamier texture. Soaking the rice is a game-changer for reducing cooking time and achieving silkier results.
*   **The Power of Broth:** Using chicken broth instead of just water will significantly enhance the depth of flavor in your congee, providing a savory foundation that complements the century egg beautifully.
*   **Stir, Stir, Stir:** Regular stirring, especially in the initial stages and towards the bottom of the pot, is crucial to prevent the rice from sticking and burning. It also helps in breaking down the rice grains more uniformly.
*   **Consistency is Key:** Congee should be thick and creamy but still pourable. If it gets too thick, don't hesitate to add more hot water or broth until you reach your desired consistency.
*   **Don't Skimp on Ginger:** Fresh ginger is not just a garnish; it plays a vital role in balancing the rich, pungent flavor of the century egg, adding a refreshing counterpoint that brightens the entire dish.

## Serving Suggestions
Congee with Century Egg is a meal in itself, but it truly shines when paired with traditional Chinese breakfast accompaniments:

*   **Youtiao (Chinese Fried Dough Sticks):** These crispy, airy fried dough sticks are perfect for dipping into the warm congee, soaking up all the delicious flavors.
*   **Pickled Vegetables:** A small side of pickled radish, mustard greens, or cucumbers offers a tangy, crunchy contrast to the creamy congee.
*   **Crispy Goodness:** A sprinkle of store-bought crispy fried shallots or garlic flakes adds an extra layer of texture and savory aroma.
*   **Flavor Boosters:** A dash of light soy sauce, a spoonful of chili oil for those who like heat, or a sprinkle of white pepper can be added at the table to customize each bowl to personal preference.

## Variations and Substitutions
One of the beauties of congee is its adaptability. While Congee with Century Egg is a classic, you can easily modify it to suit different tastes or dietary needs:

*   **Pork Alternatives:** If pork isn't your preference, shredded chicken breast or thigh makes an excellent substitute. For seafood lovers, flaked white fish (like cod or snapper) or dried scallops can be added for a different kind of umami.
*   **Vegetarian Congee:** Omit the pork and use vegetable broth. You can add sliced mushrooms (shiitake or oyster mushrooms work well), silken tofu, or other soft vegetables like zucchini or carrots for added texture and nutrients.
*   **Other Add-ins:** Get creative! Peanuts, dried shrimp, or even preserved vegetables like preserved radish (chai poh) can be stirred in for extra layers of flavor and texture.
*   **Quick Congee:** In a pinch, if you have leftover cooked rice, you can turn it into congee much faster. Just use a higher ratio of liquid and simmer until it breaks down. Many modern rice cookers also have a "congee" or "porridge" setting, making the process almost hands-off.

Congee with Century Egg is more than just a meal; it's a comforting embrace in a bowl, a taste of tradition, and a testament to the rich tapestry of Chinese culinary heritage. With this guide, you now have all the tools to bring this authentic and deeply satisfying dish to your own breakfast table. So, gather your ingredients, set aside some time, and prepare to savor the unique and heartwarming experience of homemade Congee with Century Egg. Your taste buds, and your soul, will thank you.
